events.text: Bandits catch you on a mountain road, three to one, and you are losing when someone in the black and crimson of {dvl_their_sect} drops from the pines and finishes it in four strokes. {npc} wipes the blade, looks at the badge of {dvl_my_sect} on your sleeve, and laughs. "Well. Now one of us owes the other's enemy a life."

mem.note: was bowed to by an enemy, properly

effects.log: You bow as you would to a senior of your own hall. {npc} looks startled, then bows back, badly, as if out of practice.

mem.note: was asked why, and had no answer

effects.log: "You were losing," {npc} says, "and they were ugly." It is not an answer. You think about it for a week.

choices.text: Keep your hand on your sword

mem.note: was watched like a blade by someone I saved

effects.log: You thank {him} with your hand on the hilt. {npc} notices, and seems to like you better for it.

events.text: At the lantern festival in the river town, where the sects pretend for one night that they are only people, you are buying a sugar figure when someone in the plain grey of {dvl_their_sect} reaches for the same one. {npc} does not know who you are. Your own banner, the dark side of the murim, is folded in your sleeve.

mem.note: shared a sugar crane with a stranger

effects.log: {npc} insists on halving it. You walk the length of the river eating a sugar crane together, and say nothing about sects at all.

mem.note: was told the truth at a festival

effects.log: You say the name of {dvl_my_sect} quietly. {npc} goes still, then hands you the whole sugar figure. "Tonight it does not matter," {he} says.

choices.text: Lie about where you are from

mem.note: was lied to, kindly, at a festival

effects.log: You name a merchant family from the coast. {npc} believes you. The lie sits in your sleeve beside the banner all night.

events.text: It is a duel, at first: you and a fighter of {dvl_their_sect} on a bridge, two banners, one old quarrel nobody on the bridge remembers starting. Then the rain comes down so hard you cannot see each other's blades. When it clears, {npc} is standing a hand's width away, sword lowered, and neither of you has struck.

mem.note: lowered a sword in the rain with me

effects.log: You lower it. {npc} smiles, the smile of someone who has been waiting a long time for anyone to do that.

mem.note: called a draw with me on a bridge

effects.log: You shout "A draw!" to the watchers on both banks. {npc} shouts it back. Both sides grumble and go home.

mem.note: came back to the bridge without a sword

effects.log: "Tomorrow, then," you say. {npc} nods. Tomorrow you both come back, and neither of you brings a sword.

events.text: You have never seen {npc} before, of {dvl_their_sect}, across a ferry deck in the evening. And yet your hand rises to wave before you can stop it, and {he} waves back, frowning, as if {he} has been told a story about you once and cannot remember how it ends. Something in your soul has stood on this side of the divide before.

mem.note: felt I knew someone I had never met

effects.log: You cross. "Have we met?" {npc} asks. "Not in this life," you say, and do not know why you said it.

mem.note: watched a stranger across a ferry

effects.log: You stay where you are. The ferry crosses the river, and the whole way over you can feel {him} looking.

events.text: The shrine on the border has no roof and no god, only a stone altar and the rain. {npc} is already there, drying a sword on a sleeve. Without a word {he} sets down the badge of {dvl_their_sect} on the altar. It is a question.

mem.note: laid our two badges side by side

effects.log: Two badges, side by side, on an altar no sect owns. Neither of you says anything for a long while.
{npc} looks at your sleeve, then at you, and puts the badge away again. "Next time, then," {he} says.

events.text: "Show me how your side does it," {npc} says, and takes the stance of {dvl_my_sect}, badly, on purpose, so that you will laugh and correct it. Then {he} shows you one form of {dvl_their_sect}'s, slowly, a form no outsider is meant to see. Teaching an enemy a form is a crime in both your sects.

mem.note: taught my sect's form to the other side

effects.log: You learn it. Your body stores it away in a place your own masters will never look.
"If they ever ask me, I want to be able to say no," you say. {npc} understands, and is hurt, and understands.

events.text: You are sharing a cold dumpling in the reeds when a patrol of {dvl_my_sect} comes down the river path, close enough to hear them complain about their boots. {npc} goes flat beside you in the mud. One of the patrol stops, looks straight at the reeds, and yawns.

effects.log: The patrol passes. {npc} is shaking with silent laughter. So, you find, are you.
You rise from the reeds a hundred paces off and let them chase you. {npc} gets clear; you get home soaked and very late.

events.text: The hollow in the old pine is your letterbox now. Today there is a letter from {npc}, folded small, about nothing: a dog that follows {him} to training, a cook who burns the rice, an elder who sings badly. You read it three times. It is the most dangerous thing you own.

effects.log: You burn it. You remember every word anyway, which is safer and worse.
You keep it in your boot. Anyone who searched you would hang you with it. You keep it anyway.

events.text: On a flat stone in the middle of the river, where neither bank can hear, {npc} asks you the question nobody in either sect asks: "Why do they hate us? Not the story. The reason." You open your mouth to give your elders' answer and find you do not believe it.

effects.log: "Neither do I," {npc} says. You sit with that between you, two people who do not know, and it is better than the stories.
You give it. {npc} listens politely, and gives you {dvl_their_sect}'s, which is the same story told from the other bank.

events.text: {npc} brings you something from the lands of {dvl_their_sect}: a pear, small and hard and bitter, the kind that only grows there. "Your side calls our country a wasteland," {he} says. "Eat it in front of me. I want to see your face."

mem.note: watched me eat a bitter pear

effects.log: It is terrible, and then, at the very end, sweet. {npc} watches your face and nods, satisfied, as if you passed a test.
You keep the pear in your sleeve for a month, until it is wrinkled and golden, and eat it alone.

events.text: It is {npc} who says it first, in the end, at the shrine with no roof, in the voice of someone stepping off a cliff. Then {he} waits, very straight, the way a disciple waits for a verdict. Somewhere below, {dvl_my_sect}'s evening bell is ringing for a meal you will miss.

effects.log: You say it back. The bell stops. Neither of you moves for a long time, and the rain comes in through the roof.
"I am afraid," you say. "So am I," says {npc}. "Say it anyway." You do.

events.text: You say it first, on the river stone, before you can think better of it. {npc} of {dvl_their_sect} stares at you, then puts both hands over {his} face and laughs until {he} has to wipe {his} eyes. "Every elder of mine," {he} says, "would rather see me dead. And I do not care at all."

effects.log: You take them. They are cold from the river and they hold on very hard.
"Now," says {npc}, "we are careful." You both know you will not be careful enough.

events.text: A junior of {dvl_my_sect} saw you at the border shrine. You know it the moment you walk into the hall: the silence, the way your seniors do not look at you. By evening the whole sect knows, and by the next morning, so does {dvl_their_sect}. {npc} sends one line through the pine hollow: "They know. Do not come."

effects.log: You go. {npc} is there, of course, and angry, and holds on to your sleeve as if the sects might come for you both that night.
You stay away. It is the hardest thing you have done in your life, and it changes nothing.

events.text: The letter is open on the table when you come in: {npc}'s hand, the pine hollow's fold, your own name in it. The elder of {dvl_my_sect} who intercepted it does not shout. That is worse. "{dvl_their_sect}," the elder says, as if naming a disease. "Of all the doors under heaven."

effects.log: You say nothing at all. Whatever they do with the letter, they will not get another word out of you.
"{npc} saved my life before {he} knew my name," you say. The elder writes that down too.

events.text: The elders of {dvl_my_sect} hear it in the great hall, under the banners, with every disciple watching. An envoy of {dvl_their_sect} stands at the far door, as stiff as a spear. For once both sides want the same thing. "It ends," the eldest says, "or you do. You have until the plum trees bloom three times."

effects.log: You bow to the floor. The elders take it as obedience. {dvl_name}, you think, would know it is not.
You ask. The eldest gives you a history three hundred years long. At the end of it you still do not have a reason.

events.text: {dvl_my_sect} does not hold trials. It holds a silence, and lets you stand in it until you understand. Then the hall master speaks: a disciple of the dark road who gives their heart to the righteous is a blade with a crack in it. {dvl_their_sect} has sent the same message, in fewer words. "End it. Three years."

effects.log: You do not look away. The hall master is the first to blink, and everyone in the hall sees it.
You kneel. Your knees are on the stone and your thoughts are on a border shrine with no roof.

events.text: Two envoys come to you on the same day: one from {dvl_my_sect}, one from {dvl_their_sect}, who will not sit in the same room and so stand in your courtyard at opposite corners like two herons. They deliver the same words, which neither will admit. Three years. Then the sects decide for you.

choices.text: Serve them tea from one pot

effects.log: You pour both cups from the same pot and hand them over at the same moment. Neither envoy drinks. Both notice.
They both refuse, in the same tone of voice. You laugh, and that frightens them more than anything you could have said.

events.text: There is no feast. There is a borrowed shrine, one paper lantern, an old priest who has been paid to forget your faces, and {dvl_name} in plain clothes with no badge of any sect at all. You bow to heaven, to earth, and to each other. Outside, nobody in the murim knows. Inside, it is enough.

effects.log: The priest refuses it. "I have already forgotten you," he says. "It is the only thing I do well."
You carry the lantern home under your coat. For the rest of your life it hangs where only the two of you can see it.

events.text: Married, and nobody knows. Mornings you train with {dvl_my_sect} and evenings you take the long road to a house with a red door in a town where nobody asks. {dvl_name} keeps a second set of cups. Some nights you think the secret is the best part. Some nights you think it will kill you both.

effects.log: There are more of the first kind than the second. You keep count, the way one keeps count of breaths in meditation.
You hide silver under the red door's step and a horse at the inn. Just in case.

events.text: It is not a great war, as the murim counts them: a season of ambushes, one battle on the river flats, two banners. But it is yours. And when it is over, {dvl_my_sect} and {dvl_their_sect} sign a truce on a table in the middle of the ford, and {dvl_name} is standing beside you while they do.

effects.log: Your name goes on the truce between the two seals. History will not know what to make of it.

choices.text: Walk away before the ink dries

effects.log: You leave them arguing over the wording. {dvl_name} catches up with you on the road, laughing.

events.text: The secret came out, and the sects went to war over it, and somehow, impossibly, the two of you are still standing when the smoke clears. The elders who demanded it end now demand a truce. {dvl_name} looks at you across the ford and mouths: we should have done this openly from the start.

effects.log: You should have. You will, from now on. The whole murim is going to know your names anyway.
No. The secret years were yours. You would not trade them even for this.

events.text: The war goes against you on the river flats. In the last charge, {dvl_name} steps between you and a spear meant for you, in the colours of neither sect, because by then neither sect would have them. Afterwards the truce is signed anyway. Nobody on either side can quite say what it was for.

effects.log: You carry them home yourself, all the way, and let nobody help. The road is very long.
You stand at the table in the ford, blood on your sleeves, and make both sects look at you while they sign.

events.text: The secret wedding was found out the night before it was held, and the war came of it. You lost. {dvl_name} is buried on a hill that belongs to neither sect, because you would not let either of them have the grave. There is a lantern you bought for a wedding. You light it anyway.

effects.log: You leave it on the grave, burning. It burns all night, and the next, longer than any lantern should.
You take it home. Some things should be kept, not left.

events.text: You leave at the hour of the ox, when even the gate guards of {dvl_my_sect} are asleep on their spears. {dvl_name} is waiting at the ferry with two bundles and no badge. Halfway across the river, you both take off the last thing that says what sect you belonged to, and drop it in the water.

effects.log: You watch your badge go down through the green water until you cannot see it. It does not feel like losing anything.
You keep your eyes on the far bank. {dvl_name} takes your hand. The ferryman pretends very hard not to notice.

events.text: The village at the edge of the province has never heard of {dvl_my_sect} or {dvl_their_sect}. It has heard of rain, and rice, and a fox that steals hens. You and {dvl_name} take the empty house by the bamboo, and the headman asks only whether either of you can mend a roof.

effects.log: You mend it badly the first time and well the second. The village decides you will do.

choices.text: Teach the children to fight the fox

effects.log: Within a month the fox is gone and the children are unbearable. The village forgives you.

events.text: A year after you left, a rider in the colours of {dvl_my_sect} comes through the village, asking questions. You watch from the bamboo. {dvl_name} keeps hoeing the field, a straw hat low, and does not look up. The rider asks the headman, who says there is nobody here but farmers. It is almost true now.

effects.log: The rider goes. You stand in the bamboo a long time after, until your heart slows.
You follow the rider to the next town and listen at the inn. They are giving up. You walk home lighter.

events.text: You tell {npc} at the shrine with no roof. {He} has known since you walked in. {He} does not argue. {He} takes the badge of {dvl_their_sect} out of {his} sleeve, looks at it, and puts it back. "Then be very good at what you chose," {he} says. "Make it worth this."

mem.note: was promised it would be worth it

effects.log: You promise. {npc} walks out into the rain without looking back, and you keep your promise for the rest of your life.

mem.note: was asked to hate, and could not

effects.log: "I could not if I tried," {npc} says. That is the cruellest thing anyone has ever said to you.

events.text: You end it the way the dark road ends things: quickly, without explanation, a letter in the pine hollow with one line on it. {npc} comes anyway, to the river stone, and sits there until dark. You watch from the trees and do not go down. It is the bravest and most cowardly thing you have done.

mem.note: was said goodbye to properly, in the end

effects.log: You go down. You do not change your mind. But you say goodbye properly, and {npc} thanks you for that.

mem.note: waited on the river stone for nobody

effects.log: You stay. {npc} leaves at moonrise. You sit on the stone after {he} has gone, where it is still warm.

events.text: The three years end, and the sects do not wait for your answer. {npc} is sent to a far branch hall of {dvl_their_sect} under escort; you are given a senior to follow you everywhere. You get one moment, across a market square, under the eyes of both escorts. {npc} lifts a hand. Just that.

mem.note: saw a hand lifted across a market square

effects.log: You lift your hand. Both escorts look away, as if they too had once stood in a market square.

choices.text: Turn away so they cannot use it

mem.note: watched someone turn away to protect me

effects.log: You turn away so neither sect has anything to punish. {npc} understands. It does not help.

events.text: Years into the hidden marriage, an old friend from {dvl_my_sect} visits the house with the red door, looks at the second set of cups on the shelf, and says nothing. At the gate, leaving, the friend says only: "Whoever they are, they keep your tea the way you like it. I am glad."

effects.log: You thank them. The secret is a little less heavy with one more person carrying a corner of it.
You look puzzled. Your friend smiles, bows, and never mentions it again for as long as they live.

events.text: {dvl_name} wakes you in the night to say, quite calmly, that an elder of {dvl_their_sect} was in the market today and looked twice. Nothing happens. Nothing happens the next day either. But that night you both lie awake listening to the dogs, and the hidden years feel suddenly very thin.

effects.log: You move the horse from the inn to the shed behind the house. You never need it. You are glad of it every night.
You decide it, the way one decides to stop shivering. It works, mostly.

events.text: The war over you has become a story in the teahouses, told wrongly in every province: you were a prince, {dvl_name} was a fox spirit, the river ran red, the river ran gold. A storyteller in the market tells it to a crowd while the two of you stand at the back, eating chestnuts.

effects.log: You correct one detail, loudly. The crowd turns, sees who you are, and the storyteller drops the fan.
You let it be. It is a better story the way they tell it, and yours is not for sale.

events.text: The hill that belongs to neither sect has a path to it now, worn by your own feet. Someone else has started leaving flowers on {dvl_name}'s grave as well: white ones, the kind that grow only in the lands of {dvl_their_sect}. You never see who. You leave yours beside them.

choices.text: Wait one day to see who

effects.log: You wait from dawn to dusk. Nobody comes. The next morning there are fresh white flowers anyway.
You leave a note under a stone: Thank you. The next time, there is a note under the stone for you: Thank you too.

events.text: The children of the village by the bamboo think you were always farmers. One of them, practising with a stick behind the house, does a form of {dvl_their_sect}'s so perfectly that you drop the basket you are holding. {dvl_name} has been teaching. Of course {dvl_name} has been teaching.

choices.text: Teach the child a form of your own

effects.log: You teach one of {dvl_my_sect}'s forms, beside it. The child does both, side by side, with no idea they were ever enemies.
You ask. {dvl_name} agrees. Both of you know the child will remember anyway.

events.text: Years later, at a festival in a town neither sect owns, you see {dvl_name} across the lantern street: older, laughing at something, a child on one hip who is not yours and could never have been. {dvl_name} sees you too. The street is too wide, and also not wide at all.

effects.log: You raise a hand. {dvl_name} raises one back. Then the crowd closes between you, and that is the whole of it, and it is enough.
You turn away before either of you can decide anything. Your heart beats wrong for the rest of the night.

events.text: News reaches you, late, the way news does: {dvl_name} is dead, of a fever, far away in the lands of {dvl_their_sect}. Nobody from either sect thinks to tell you directly. It comes as a line in a merchant's gossip, between the price of salt and a wedding you do not care about.

effects.log: You light one stick, alone, facing the direction of a country you have never been allowed to see.

choices.text: Go back to the border shrine

effects.log: You climb to the shrine with no roof. The altar is still there. You sit on it until the rain comes.
